## 1. Traditional reading

**Background (vv. 23–33 as a whole)**
- Henry says the Sadducees believed nothing spiritual exists except God, only matter and motion. They also didn't accept the prophets as inspired, only what God himself spoke at Sinai. They opposed Jesus because his teaching took the resurrection further than earlier revelation had. (MH)
- Henry notes that the Pharisees and Sadducees disagreed with each other but joined forces against Christ. He compares them to superstitious hypocrites on one side and unbelievers on the other: both keep or mock the outward form of religion while denying its power. (MH)
- Wuest (quoted on PA) says "Teacher" was only a polite formality. They came to trap Jesus with a "resurrection riddle," not to learn. (PA)

**v. 29**
- Guzik sees two causes for their mistake. First, they didn't really know the Scriptures, though they thought they did. Second, they didn't know God's power, because at root they rejected the supernatural. (EW)
- He adds that someone can know a lot of Bible facts and still miss the pattern of sound doctrine that runs through Scripture. (EW, summary)
- Henry says faith rests on God's power, bound to his promise. He argues that Scripture plainly teaches the soul lives on and that both the just and the unjust will be raised, pointing to Job and Ezekiel. (MH)

**v. 30**
- Guzik: resurrection life is not this life carried on. It is a completely different kind of life. If it seems to lack some earthly pleasures, that is because heaven's joys are far greater. (EW)
- Guzik on practical comfort: many people in heaven will have had more than one spouse, and Jesus shows there will be no jealousy or shutting anyone out there. (EW)
- Guzik, quoting Carson: simply by mentioning angels, Jesus affirmed they are real, and the Sadducees denied that. (EW)
- Preceptaustin: people will be like angels because they will live forever. With no death, there is no longer any need to have children to keep the human race going. (PA)

**v. 31**
- Spurgeon: Jesus always deeply respected God's written Word. Saying God spoke "to you" shows that Scripture speaks personally to each reader. God said these words to these very Sadducees, even though they didn't realise it. (SP)

**v. 32**
- Guzik: Jesus proved the resurrection from the five books of Moses alone, because those were the only books the Sadducees accepted. He also points to the tense: God says "I am" the God of Abraham, not "I was." (EW)
- Spurgeon: the patriarchs had been dead a long time when God spoke from the burning bush. His words implied they were still alive, because his covenant was with people who still exist. (SP)
- Henry: if no happiness awaited the patriarchs after death, Jacob's sad remark that his days were "few and evil" would be a lasting reproach to God's faithfulness. So there must be a future state. And if the soul lives on, the body must one day live again with it. (MH)

**vv. 35–36**
- Guzik: this question was also a trap. By making Jesus pick one great commandment, they hoped to show he neglected another part of the law. (EW)

**vv. 37–38**
- Guzik: Jesus didn't rank one command above another. He summed up the law in its core principles: love the Lord with everything you have, and love your neighbour as yourself. (EW)
- A Guzik Q&A page treats loving God as something God commands, quoting vv. 37–38. (https://enduringword.com/how-can-i-love-god-more-live-qa-for-march-24-2022/)

**v. 39**
- Guzik links this verse to treating others the way you'd want to be treated, the "golden rule." That name isn't in Scripture but is the common term for it. He notes some teachers in Jesus' day took the command to mean "love my neighbour and hate my enemy," which Jesus clearly rejected. (https://enduringword.com/how-do-i-love-someone-who-is-really-wrong-live-qa-with-david-guzik-for-august-24-2023-2/)
- On "as yourself," Preceptaustin uses the Good Samaritan. The men who passed by didn't fail from loving themselves too little but from loving themselves too much, putting their own interests first. True love looks outward. The excerpt doesn't say who wrote this part. (PA)

**v. 40**
- Guzik: these two sentences sum up, briefly and powerfully, everything God morally expects of people. All the Law and the Prophets come from love for God and love for neighbour. (EW)

**vv. 43–45**
- Guzik: Jesus moves his opponents from a partial truth (the Christ is David's son) to the whole truth (he is also David's Lord), which shows he is God. (EW, summary)

**v. 44**
- Spurgeon: "Sit at My right hand" means the Messiah rests after finishing his work as mediator, in the place of honour, power and majesty. He keeps that seat until all his enemies are defeated at his feet. (SP)
